title: How the Water Cycle Moves Water Around Earth
description: How water evaporates, condenses, falls and flows back to the ocean, from USGS and NASA.
narration: Where does the rain that falls today go next? The water cycle is the story of where Earth's water is stored and how it moves between those places. Sunlight and gravity keep that water moving all the time. Evaporation from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers supplies nearly 90% of the moisture in the air. Plants release most of the rest through tiny pores in their leaves, a process called transpiration. Rising air currents carry water vapor high into the atmosphere, where cool air makes condensation into cloud droplets more likely, and precipitation carries the water back to the surface. Over land, precipitation can evaporate back to the atmosphere, seep into the ground, or run off into rivers and streams, and almost all of the water eventually reaches the oceans. Oceans hold about 96% of all the water on Earth. At any moment the air holds only 12,900 cubic kilometers of water, a minute fraction of Earth's total, yet roughly 495,000 cubic kilometers cycle through it each year.

claims.sentence: The water cycle is the story of where Earth's water is stored and how it moves between those places.
claims.quote: The water cycle describes where water is on Earth and how it moves. Water is stored in the atmosphere, on the land surface, and below the ground.

claims.sentence: Sunlight and gravity keep that water moving all the time.
claims.quote: Energy from the sun and the force of gravity drive the continual movement of water between pools.

claims.sentence: Evaporation from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers supplies nearly 90% of the moisture in the air.
claims.quote: Studies have revealed that evaporation—the process by which water changes from a liquid to a gas—from oceans, seas, and other bodies of water (lakes, rivers, streams) provides nearly 90% of the moisture in our atmosphere.

claims.sentence: Plants release most of the rest through tiny pores in their leaves, a process called transpiration.
claims.quote: Most of the remaining 10% found in the atmosphere is released by plants through transpiration. Plants take in water through their roots, then release it through small pores on the underside of their leaves.

claims.sentence: Rising air currents carry water vapor high into the atmosphere, where cool air makes condensation into cloud droplets more likely, and precipitation carries the water back to the surface.
claims.quote: rising air currents carry it upward, often high into the atmosphere, where the air is cooler. In the cool air, water vapor is more likely to condense from a gas to a liquid to form cloud droplets. Cloud droplets can grow and produce precipitation (including rain, snow, sleet, freezing rain, and hail), which is the primary mechanism for transporting water from the atmosphere back to the Earth’s surface.

claims.sentence: Over land, precipitation can evaporate back to the atmosphere, seep into the ground, or run off into rivers and streams, and almost all of the water eventually reaches the oceans.
claims.quote: Some of it evaporates, returning to the atmosphere; some seeps into the ground as soil moisture or groundwater; and some runs off into rivers and streams. Almost all of the water eventually flows into the oceans or other bodies of water, where the cycle continues.

claims.sentence: Oceans hold about 96% of all the water on Earth.
claims.quote: Oceans store 96% of all water on Earth.

claims.sentence: At any moment the air holds only 12,900 cubic kilometers of water, a minute fraction of Earth's total, yet roughly 495,000 cubic kilometers cycle through it each year.
claims.quote: The amount of water in the atmosphere at any moment in time is only 12,900 cubic kilometers, a minute fraction of Earth’s total water supply: if it were to completely rain out, atmospheric moisture would cover the Earth’s surface to a depth of only 2.5 centimeters. However, far more water—in fact, some 495,000 cubic kilometers of it—are cycled through the atmosphere every year.

scenes.narration_segment: Water moves between the atmosphere, land and ocean, driven by sunlight and gravity.
Evaporation supplies nearly 90% of atmospheric moisture, plants most of the rest.
Vapour condenses into clouds, falls as rain or snow and runs back to the ocean.
Oceans hold about 96% of Earth's water, and the air holds a tiny fraction.
